Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Indexing Strategies
Indexing Strategies and Performance Optimization
Understand explain(), design indexes for covered queries, and use sparse / TTL indexes safely in production.
In this lesson

You will diagnose slow queries with explain(), build compound indexes for coverage, use sparse and TTL indexes for special cases, and apply ESR ordering plus monitoring to production systems.

Why it matters

Well-designed indexes reduce disk I/O, lower latency, and keep write cost acceptable. Indexes are a performance lever that must be tuned as data grows.

Explore Key Topics
explain()
Inspect winningPlan, IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, and execution metrics to find indexing gaps.
Index Design
Create compound indexes, follow ESR ordering, and prefer covered queries to avoid document fetches.
Special Indexes
Use sparse indexes for optional fields and TTL indexes for automatic expiration of time-based data.
Visual Summary
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Explain output
winningPlan, keys examined, docs examined, execution time.
Covered Query
All projected and filtered fields in the index—no FETCH required.
TTL & Sparse
Automatic expiry; sparse skips missing fields.
Lab preview

You'll run explain on a slow query, add a compound index to convert a COLLSCAN into an IXSCAN, demonstrate a covered query, create a sparse unique index for optional userId, and add a TTL index to expire old logs.

screens.title: Using explain() to diagnose queries
screens.narratorSegment: Explain is the diagnostic lens into MongoDB’s decision-making. When you append explain("executionStats") to a query, you get a structured report describing the chosen plan and detailed metrics like totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined, nReturned, and executionTimeMillis. Start by finding the winningPlan. stage: IXSCAN shows an index was used, COLLSCAN indicates a full collection scan, and FETCH appears when MongoDB needs to retrieve documents after locating keys. A practical workflow is to run explain on your slow query, note whether it used IXSCAN, and check how many documents and keys were examined relative to results returned. For example, running db. products. find({ "category": "Electronics" }). explain("executionStats") shows whether a category index exists and how effective it is. A high totalDocsExamined to nReturned ratio signals a poor filter or missing index. Use those metrics to choose a compound index that narrows results earlier. A common misconception is to judge success by executionTimeMillis alone; timing can vary with load and cache. Instead, focus on IXSCAN presence and low examined-to-returned ratios as stable signs of index effectiveness. Try asking: does the winning plan avoid scanning the whole collection?

keyIdea.title: Explain workflow
keyIdea.text: Run explain("executionStats"), inspect winningPlan.stage and examined metrics, and prioritize plans that use IXSCAN with low docs-examined per returned document.

content.html:
Core Concept
Using explain() to diagnose queries
See which plan ran and measure index effectiveness with stable metrics.
Key explain() metrics
  • winningPlan.stage: IXSCAN, COLLSCAN, FETCH — the execution steps used.
  • totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined: show how much work the query did.
  • executionTimeMillis: overall elapsed time; useful but variable with system load.
Common pitfall
Relying only on elapsed time can mislead — focus on index usage and examined ratios instead.
Check your work
After adding an index, re-run explain and confirm winningPlan shows IXSCAN and that totalDocsExamined drops close to nReturned.
Example
Run explain on a category filter to confirm an index is used.
<pre><code>db.products.find({ "category": "Electronics" }).explain("executionStats") </code></pre>
Interpretation checklist
  • Is winningPlan.stage IXSCAN? If not, consider an index.
  • Is totalDocsExamined near nReturned? If not, refine index or filter.
  • Are many keys examined? Consider a more selective index ordering.
Key Takeaway

Explain gives you stable signals — winning plan type and examined counts — to base indexing decisions on, not just elapsed time.

screens.title: Understanding winningPlan stages: IXSCAN, COLLSCAN, FETCH
screens.narratorSegment: The winningPlan stages in explain show the operations used to satisfy a query. IXSCAN means MongoDB used an index to scan matching keys; this is generally what you want for filtered queries. COLLSCAN indicates a full collection scan: every document was checked against the filter, often a signal that an index is missing or mismatched. FETCH appears when the engine must retrieve the full document after identifying candidate keys — typically because the projection requested fields outside the index. Knowing these stages helps you choose the right fix. If you see COLLSCAN, create a suitable index for the filter pattern. If you see IXSCAN followed by FETCH, consider turning the query into a covered query by including projected fields in the index. A common misconception is that IXSCAN always eliminates disk reads. It does reduce key scanning, but if FETCH is present you still access documents. For example, a filter on status with an index on status alone will IXSCAN, but if you project a non-indexed message field you will see FETCH. The practical answer is to inspect the stages, then either add the missing projected field to the compound index or adjust your projection to fields already indexed.

keyIdea.title: Stage meanings
keyIdea.text: IXSCAN: index used; COLLSCAN: full scan; FETCH: documents fetched because projection or other data was not in the index.

content.html:
Definition
winningPlan stages
Decode IXSCAN, COLLSCAN, and FETCH to guide index changes.
IXSCAN
Index scan over keys. Good for filtered queries. Lower keys examined is desirable.
COLLSCAN
Full collection scan. Usually a sign an index is missing for the filter and should be addressed for performance.
FETCH
MongoDB must fetch full documents when the index alone cannot satisfy the projection or other required fields.
Concrete example
Index on status only; projection requests message.
db.logs.find({ "status": "ERROR" }, { "message": 1 }).explain("executionStats")
This will likely show IXSCAN then FETCH because message is not in the status index. Make the index cover message too to avoid FETCH.
Pro tip

When you see FETCH often, aim for a covered index or reduce projections to indexed fields to eliminate document fetches and reduce I/O.

screens.title: Metrics to watch: totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, executionTimeMillis
screens.narratorSegment: Three metrics carry the most diagnostic weight: totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined, and executionTimeMillis. Keys examined measures how many index entries were scanned. Documents examined tells you how many full documents were retrieved or checked. Execution time is the overall elapsed time. A healthy indexed query usually shows relatively low totalKeysExamined and a totalDocsExamined close to nReturned. If keys examined is high but docs examined low, the index limits candidate documents but additional filtering is pruning results. If docs examined is much larger than nReturned, MongoDB is checking many documents to satisfy the query—this often indicates a missing or poorly ordered index. When you change indexes, follow a small-process: run explain, add the index, re-run explain, and compare the metrics. Keep an eye on executionTimeMillis but prioritize stable signals (examined counts) because time varies with server load and cache warmness. A common mistake is to add many indexes to chase microsecond gains; that increases write cost and memory usage. Aim to optimize the slowest, most frequent queries and remove unused indexes after monitoring with indexStats. Metrics to watch: totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, executionTimeMillis means compare totaldocsexamined to nreturned and aim to keep keys and docs examined low; use explain before and after index changes to measure impact.. In practical terms, how to interpret ratios and diagnose inefficiencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Metric triage
keyIdea.text: Compare totalDocsExamined to nReturned and aim to keep keys and docs examined low; use explain before and after index changes to measure impact.

content.html:
Process Flow
Metric triage for explain()
Use a short compare-and-validate process when tuning indexes.
Step 1 — Baseline
Run explain("executionStats") and record keys/documents examined and nReturned.
Step 2 — Index
Create a candidate index designed for the filter and projection, following ESR ordering.
Step 3 — Verify
Re-run explain and compare metrics. Look for IXSCAN and lower totalDocsExamined relative to nReturned.
Example insight
If totalDocsExamined is 1000 and nReturned is 2, many documents are being read to find matches—add a selective index to narrow the scan earlier.
Common mistake
Adding indexes for every field you think might help. Excess indexes slow writes and increase memory; optimize the hot paths first.
Key Takeaway

Use examined-to-returned ratios and winningPlan stages as the primary signals for index effectiveness; execution time is secondary but still useful.

screens.title: Covered queries: how to avoid FETCH
screens.narratorSegment: A covered query is one where MongoDB can satisfy the filter, projection, and sort entirely from an index without fetching documents. This is the fastest possible read path because it avoids disk input and output to retrieve full documents. To design covered queries, include all fields used in the predicate and the projected fields in the same index. For example, with an index { "category": 1, "name": 1, "price": 1 }, the query db. products. find({ "category": "Electronics" }, { "name": 1, "price": 1, "_id": 0 }) can be covered because category is in the index and both projected fields are present. Remember that _id is included in every index; projecting _id is fine. A common misconception is thinking any compound index provides coverage — projections must match indexed fields exactly. Also, coverage has trade-offs: wider indexes consume more space and memory, so use them where reads benefit most. When coverage is practical, you will see IXSCAN without FETCH in explain output and a dramatic reduction in totalDocsExamined. Ask yourself whether the projected fields truly need to be returned in every query before expanding indexes to achieve coverage.

keyIdea.title: Covered query rule
keyIdea.text: Include all predicate, projection, and sort fields in the index to avoid FETCH and deliver the fastest reads.

content.html:
Comparison
Covered queries vs non-covered
When possible, prefer covered queries for the lowest latency reads.
Covered query example
db.products.createIndex({ "category": 1, "name": 1, "price": 1 })
db.products.find({ "category": "Electronics" }, { "name": 1, "price": 1, "_id": 0 })
// explain("executionStats") should show IXSCAN without FETCH
Coverage avoids document fetches. Only project fields that are indexed to keep indexes small when possible.
Trade-offs
  • Wider indexes increase disk and RAM usage.
  • Indexes with low selectivity waste space; prefer selective fields first in ESR order.
  • Use covered indexes where reads dominate and latency matters most.
Check your understanding

If a projection returns a field not in the index, will the query be covered? No — explain will show FETCH. Can _id be part of coverage? Yes, _id exists in every index.

screens.title: Index intersection: when multiple indexes combine
screens.narratorSegment: Index intersection occurs when MongoDB uses two or more single-field indexes and intersects the matching _id sets to satisfy a multi-predicate query. This can be useful if you lack a compound index that matches the query, and it sometimes yields good performance by narrowing results via separate selective indexes. For example, with indexes on { "status": 1 } and { "city": 1 }, a query db. users. find({ "status": "active", "city": "New York" }) might use index intersection. However, intersection is a fallback: creating a well-ordered compound index often performs better and avoids extra intersection work. Design for intersection only when a compound index would be too costly or when predicates vary widely. A common misconception is that intersection always matches the performance of a compound index; it usually does not. Use explain to see whether MongoDB intersected indexes by checking winningPlan details. If intersection appears but still examines many documents, prefer a compound index ordered by ESR to directly support the query pattern. Remember to balance index count and write cost when adding compound indexes. Index intersection: when multiple indexes combine means index intersection can combine multiple single-field indexes, but a single compound index ordered by esr is usually preferable for consistent query patterns.. In practical terms, how mongodb intersects index results and when to prefer a compound index. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Intersection vs compound
keyIdea.text: Index intersection can combine multiple single-field indexes, but a single compound index ordered by ESR is usually preferable for consistent query patterns.

content.html:
Comparison
Index Intersection
MongoDB may intersect multiple indexes when no single compound index covers the query.
Example
With separate indexes on {"status":1} and {"city":1}, the query below might use index intersection:
db.users.find({ "status": "active", "city": "New York" }).explain("executionStats")
When to prefer compound
  • Query pattern is common and predictable: create a compound index ordered for that shape.
  • Intersection may be slower if many documents match the separate indexes before intersection.
  • Compound indexes reduce work by scanning a single index in order.
Check

If explain shows index intersection but examined counts remain high, design a compound index using ESR order to directly serve the query.

screens.title: Sparse indexes and conditional uniqueness
screens.narratorSegment: Sparse indexes include only documents that contain the indexed field. They’re useful when a field is optional and you want to index or enforce uniqueness only for documents that actually have a value. For example, if user documents sometimes include phoneNumber and you want a unique constraint for provided numbers but allow many users without a phone number, create a sparse unique index: db. users. createIndex({ "phoneNumber": 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true }). This ensures documents missing phoneNumber are not indexed and therefore do not conflict with uniqueness. Be cautious: sparse indexes can complicate queries that expect to find documents missing a field. They also interact with partialFilterExpression patterns in newer index options; however, sparse remains a concise way to ignore absent fields. A common misconception is that sparse indexes speed up all queries involving the field — they only index fewer entries, which can reduce index size, but selectivity and query patterns still determine performance. Use explain to confirm your query uses the sparse index when the field is present, and run indexStats to measure usage. Sparse indexes and conditional uniqueness means use sparse indexes to include only documents with the field, enabling uniqueness or smaller indexes for optional attributes.. In practical terms, index only documents that contain the field to handle optional attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sparse index rule
keyIdea.text: Use sparse indexes to include only documents with the field, enabling uniqueness or smaller indexes for optional attributes.

content.html:
Definition
Sparse indexes
Index only documents that include the indexed field, useful for optional values and conditional uniqueness.
Example
db.users.createIndex({ "phoneNumber": 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true })
This enforces uniqueness for users who provide phoneNumber while allowing many users with no phoneNumber field.
Caveats
  • Queries that expect documents without the field may not use the sparse index.
  • Sparse indexes reduce index size but do not replace careful selectivity and ordering considerations.
Check your understanding

Do sparse indexes include nulls? They include only documents that contain the field; behavior with explicit null values depends on presence and indexing rules.

screens.title: TTL indexes for automatic expiration
screens.narratorSegment: TTL indexes remove documents automatically after a specified time interval based on a BSON date field. They’re ideal for sessions, caches, and log records where data becomes stale. Create a TTL index on a date field and set expireAfterSeconds. For example, db. sessions. createIndex({ "createdAt": 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }) will expire documents one hour after their createdAt timestamp. Remember that the background TTL monitor runs periodically, roughly every minute, so expiration is not instantaneous. Also note that the _id field cannot be used for TTL. TTL indexes can also improve queries that filter by the date field because an index exists, but their primary role is lifecycle management. A common misconception is that TTL indexes enforce exact deletion timing; they are approximate due to the periodic background process. For production, choose expireAfterSeconds that match your business retention and verify behavior in a non-production environment before deploying to live traffic. content.html:
Definition
TTL indexes
Expire documents automatically by date using expireAfterSeconds on a single date field.
Example
db.sessions.createIndex({ "createdAt": 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 })
This expires sessions one hour after the createdAt timestamp. Expect deletions to occur on the TTL monitor cycle.
Important notes
  • The TTL background process runs periodically, so expiration timing is approximate.
  • The indexed field must hold BSON date values for TTL to work.
  • _id cannot be used for a TTL index.
Why it matters

TTL indexes simplify lifecycle management for ephemeral data and help keep collections small without manual deletion jobs.

screens.title: Index design rules: ESR and selectivity
screens.narratorSegment: A compact guideline for compound indexes is ESR: place equality fields first, then sort fields, and finally range fields. Equality fields narrow the result set immediately, sort fields allow an index to satisfy ordering without an additional SORT stage, and range fields must come last because they break prefix usage of subsequent keys. Also prioritize selectivity: index fields that significantly reduce candidate documents will have the biggest impact. For example, if you frequently query where category equals X and then sort by price, an index { category: 1, price: 1 } follows ESR and supports both the filter and the sort. Avoid indexing low-selectivity boolean flags if they do not meaningfully reduce results. When choosing between multiple possible compound keys, focus on the most common query pattern in your workload. Remember too that every additional index increases write cost and consumes R A M. Use indexStats to measure usage frequency and prune indexes that are rarely used. A common misconception is to index every field used anywhere; instead, index the hot paths and remove unused indexes after monitoring. Index design rules: ESR and selectivity means order fields as equality → sort → range and choose selective fields first to get the best compound index performance.. In practical terms, order compound index fields with equality → sort → range and pick selective keys first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ESR rule
keyIdea.text: Order fields as Equality → Sort → Range and choose selective fields first to get the best compound index performance.

content.html:
Best Practices
ESR: Equality → Sort → Range
A simple ordering rule to maximize index usefulness for common query shapes.
Why ESR matters
  • Equality first: immediately narrow candidate set.
  • Sort second: allow index to satisfy sort without extra work.
  • Range last: preserves index prefixes for equality and sort keys.
Concrete example
If queries commonly use category equality and sort by price, create { "category": 1, "price": 1 } not { "price": 1, "category": 1 } to support both filter and sort.
Selectivity note
Pick index keys that narrow results efficiently. Fields with many distinct values give better selectivity than low-cardinality flags.
Key Takeaway

Follow ESR ordering and prioritize selective keys to design compound indexes that support common query shapes and sorts.

screens.title: Index management in production
screens.narratorSegment: Managing indexes in production requires monitoring, caution, and a plan. Use db. collection. aggregate([ { $indexStats: {} } ]) to see which indexes are used and how often; prune indexes that show near-zero usage to reduce write overhead and memory pressure. Build large indexes in the background to avoid blocking operations on large collections using createIndex with background: true. Remember that too many indexes slow writes and increase disk and R A M consumption, so balance read performance gains against write costs. Also ensure your working set and indexes fit in R A M for predictable low-latency reads. When deploying index changes, run explain on critical queries before and after the change and monitor application metrics. A common mistake is creating indexes for rare ad-hoc queries; instead, prioritize indexes for frequent, high-latency queries. Use indexStats and explain together: explain shows plan level details, indexStats shows usage over time. Finally, schedule index cleanups as part of maintenance to reclaim space and keep operational costs predictable. Index management in production
Monitor usage, prune, and build safely to keep performance predictable.

db.collection.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }])

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to read MongoDB query plans, design indexes that actually speed queries, and use specialized index types for lifecycle and sparsely populated fields. We start with explain, the diagnostic method that surfaces winning plans, index usage, and key metrics like totalDocsExamined and executionTimeMillis. Then we move into practical design: compound indexes that support covered queries, when index intersection helps, and how sparse indexes let you enforce uniqueness only when a field exists. We also cover TTL indexes to automate expiration for session and log data. Finally, you'll get production-focused guidance: how to monitor index usage, avoid over-indexing, and keep indexes sized for R A M. As you work, you'll practice using explain("executionStats") to confirm index effects and apply ESR ordering for compound keys. By the end of this lesson you’ll understand not only which index to create, but why it improves performance and which trade-offs to watch for.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to inspect query plans with explain() and interpret metrics like winningPlan. stage, totalDocsExamined, and totalKeysExamined so you can locate index-related bottlenecks. You will design compound indexes to support common queries and produce covered queries that eliminate document fetches, improving latency. You will also implement and reason about sparse indexes when fields are optional, and create TTL indexes to automate data cleanup for session or log data. Each objective focuses on practical, exam-relevant skills: using explain for diagnosis, ordering keys with ESR for compound indexes, choosing when index intersection is helpful, and applying production safeguards like background builds and index usage monitoring. Along the way you’ll practice a lab that walks through creating indexes and re-running explain to observe the performance change, so you can demonstrate competency with real output.

These objectives expand into operational skills you will use daily: create TTL indexes to expire old documents automatically and tune expireAfterSeconds for your retention needs. You will apply ESR ordering — placing equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields — so compound indexes match common query shapes. You'll learn to monitor index usage with the indexStats aggregation and to avoid over-indexing, balancing read performance with write cost and disk usage. Finally, you'll practice background index creation and strategies to keep indexes sized for R A M. Each objective includes a compact mnemonic or visual to help you remember when and why to use the technique. The lab will combine these skills: create the proper indexes, re-run explain("executionStats"), and verify improvements using the metrics discussed earlier. Learning Objectives — continued means create ttl indexes, apply esr ordering, monitor index usage, and manage index cost in production.. In practical terms, production skills and applied tuning. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Explain is the diagnostic lens into MongoDB’s decision-making. When you append explain("executionStats") to a query, you get a structured report describing the chosen plan and detailed metrics like totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined, nReturned, and executionTimeMillis. Start by finding the winningPlan. stage: IXSCAN shows an index was used, COLLSCAN indicates a full collection scan, and FETCH appears when MongoDB needs to retrieve documents after locating keys. A practical workflow is to run explain on your slow query, note whether it used IXSCAN, and check how many documents and keys were examined relative to results returned. For example, running db. products. find({ "category": "Electronics" }). explain("executionStats") shows whether a category index exists and how effective it is. A high totalDocsExamined to nReturned ratio signals a poor filter or missing index. Use those metrics to choose a compound index that narrows results earlier. A common misconception is to judge success by executionTimeMillis alone; timing can vary with load and cache. Instead, focus on IXSCAN presence and low examined-to-returned ratios as stable signs of index effectiveness. Try asking: does the winning plan avoid scanning the whole collection?

The winningPlan stages in explain show the operations used to satisfy a query. IXSCAN means MongoDB used an index to scan matching keys; this is generally what you want for filtered queries. COLLSCAN indicates a full collection scan: every document was checked against the filter, often a signal that an index is missing or mismatched. FETCH appears when the engine must retrieve the full document after identifying candidate keys — typically because the projection requested fields outside the index. Knowing these stages helps you choose the right fix. If you see COLLSCAN, create a suitable index for the filter pattern. If you see IXSCAN followed by FETCH, consider turning the query into a covered query by including projected fields in the index. A common misconception is that IXSCAN always eliminates disk reads. It does reduce key scanning, but if FETCH is present you still access documents. For example, a filter on status with an index on status alone will IXSCAN, but if you project a non-indexed message field you will see FETCH. The practical answer is to inspect the stages, then either add the missing projected field to the compound index or adjust your projection to fields already indexed.

Three metrics carry the most diagnostic weight: totalKeysExamined, totalDocsExamined, and executionTimeMillis. Keys examined measures how many index entries were scanned. Documents examined tells you how many full documents were retrieved or checked. Execution time is the overall elapsed time. A healthy indexed query usually shows relatively low totalKeysExamined and a totalDocsExamined close to nReturned. If keys examined is high but docs examined low, the index limits candidate documents but additional filtering is pruning results. If docs examined is much larger than nReturned, MongoDB is checking many documents to satisfy the query—this often indicates a missing or poorly ordered index. When you change indexes, follow a small-process: run explain, add the index, re-run explain, and compare the metrics. Keep an eye on executionTimeMillis but prioritize stable signals (examined counts) because time varies with server load and cache warmness. A common mistake is to add many indexes to chase microsecond gains; that increases write cost and memory usage. Aim to optimize the slowest, most frequent queries and remove unused indexes after monitoring with indexStats. Metrics to watch: totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, executionTimeMillis means compare totaldocsexamined to nreturned and aim to keep keys and docs examined low; use explain before and after index changes to measure impact.. In practical terms, how to interpret ratios and diagnose inefficiencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A covered query is one where MongoDB can satisfy the filter, projection, and sort entirely from an index without fetching documents. This is the fastest possible read path because it avoids disk input and output to retrieve full documents. To design covered queries, include all fields used in the predicate and the projected fields in the same index. For example, with an index { "category": 1, "name": 1, "price": 1 }, the query db. products. find({ "category": "Electronics" }, { "name": 1, "price": 1, "_id": 0 }) can be covered because category is in the index and both projected fields are present. Remember that _id is included in every index; projecting _id is fine. A common misconception is thinking any compound index provides coverage — projections must match indexed fields exactly. Also, coverage has trade-offs: wider indexes consume more space and memory, so use them where reads benefit most. When coverage is practical, you will see IXSCAN without FETCH in explain output and a dramatic reduction in totalDocsExamined. Ask yourself whether the projected fields truly need to be returned in every query before expanding indexes to achieve coverage.

Index intersection occurs when MongoDB uses two or more single-field indexes and intersects the matching _id sets to satisfy a multi-predicate query. This can be useful if you lack a compound index that matches the query, and it sometimes yields good performance by narrowing results via separate selective indexes. For example, with indexes on { "status": 1 } and { "city": 1 }, a query db. users. find({ "status": "active", "city": "New York" }) might use index intersection. However, intersection is a fallback: creating a well-ordered compound index often performs better and avoids extra intersection work. Design for intersection only when a compound index would be too costly or when predicates vary widely. A common misconception is that intersection always matches the performance of a compound index; it usually does not. Use explain to see whether MongoDB intersected indexes by checking winningPlan details. If intersection appears but still examines many documents, prefer a compound index ordered by ESR to directly support the query pattern. Sparse indexes include only documents that contain the indexed field. They’re useful when a field is optional and you want to index or enforce uniqueness only for documents that actually have a value. For example, if user documents sometimes include phoneNumber and you want a unique constraint for provided numbers but allow many users without a phone number, create a sparse unique index: db. users. createIndex({ "phoneNumber": 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true }). This ensures documents missing phoneNumber are not indexed and therefore do not conflict with uniqueness. Be cautious: sparse indexes can complicate queries that expect to find documents missing a field. They also interact with partialFilterExpression patterns in newer index options; however, sparse remains a concise way to ignore absent fields. TTL indexes remove documents automatically after a specified time interval based on a BSON date field. They’re ideal for sessions, caches, and log records where data becomes stale. Create a TTL index on a date field and set expireAfterSeconds. For example, db. sessions. createIndex({ "createdAt": 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }) will expire documents one hour after their createdAt timestamp. Remember that the background TTL monitor runs periodically, roughly every minute, so expiration is not instantaneous. Also note that the _id field cannot be used for TTL. A compact guideline for compound indexes is ESR: place equality fields first, then sort fields, and finally range fields. Equality fields narrow the result set immediately, sort fields allow an index to satisfy ordering without an additional SORT stage, and range fields must come last because they break prefix usage of subsequent keys. Also prioritize selectivity: index fields that significantly reduce candidate documents will have the biggest impact. For example, if you frequently query where category equals X and then sort by price, an index { category: 1, price: 1 } follows ESR and supports both the filter and the sort. Avoid indexing low-selectivity boolean flags if they do not meaningfully reduce results.
